verses.1: Al-Mizan states: Guard against your Lord’s punishment: the earthquake of the Hour is grievous.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan introduces Sūrah al-Ḥajj as a Medinan chapter of seventy-eight verses, apparently revealed after the migration but before Badr, when the polytheists still had power and the believers had newly formed a community with the means to fight. It warns the polytheists about Islam’s fundamental beliefs and instructs believers concerning prayer, hajj, good conduct, and permission for jihād. Its purpose is to set out the fundamental beliefs for both groups and religious practices concisely for believers; detailed rulings had not yet generally been prescribed, apart from matters such as prayer and hajj. Its opening depiction of Resurrection and the preceding earthquake that destroys the earth and mountains serves both to warn the polytheists and to call believers to fear and consciousness of God.

The commentary explains that zalzalah and zilzāl mean a violent, terrifying movement. Zalzalah is likely derived from zalla, “to slip,” and its repeated form conveys both intensity and recurrence. The address to “people” encompasses all humanity—believers and non-believers, male and female, those present at revelation and those to come—though those present were its primary audience. Guarding against the Lord’s punishment means believing for the non-believer and obeying God’s injunctions in practice for the believer. The gravity of the Hour’s earthquake grounds this warning. The quake is one of the signs of the Hour; the proposed interpretation of zalzalat al-sāʿah as merely the Hour’s intensity, violence, and horror is unlikely because zalzalah denotes an actual violent movement.

Al-Mizan explains dhuhūl as abandoning something out of fear. Al-Rāghib distinguishes ḥaml, a burden carried within, such as a fetus, from ḥiml, carried outwardly, such as a camel’s load; Majmaʿ al-bayān likewise treats ḥaml as what is inside the body or on a tree, and ḥiml as what is borne on the back or head. Al-Kashshāf reports that murḍiʿah denotes a woman actually suckling at that moment, unlike murḍiʿ, which denotes one who performs the task without necessarily doing so then. The wording therefore heightens the terror: even a mother with her breast in her infant’s mouth will withdraw it in fright.

The plural “you shall see” concerns the quake, seen by everyone, whereas the singular concerns each person seeing other people as though intoxicated. The verse first affirms and then denies their intoxication: terror and confusion disable their intellects, not wine, because Allah’s chastisement is severe—“Surely His punishment is painful, severe. (11:102)” Apparently this earthquake occurs before the first blast of the Trumpet, described in “And the trumpet shall be blown, so all those that are in the heavens and all those that are on the earth shall swoon, except those whom Allah wills; then it shall be blown again, then lo! They shall stand, waiting. (39:68)” People are living ordinarily when the earthquake suddenly overtakes and transforms them, and it certainly precedes the blast that kills all living creatures. The suggestion that the scene is only a hypothetical illustration of punishment’s severity is rejected: warning people of an unknown chastisement would serve no purpose.
verses.3: Al-Mizan depicts one who disputes about Allah ignorantly and follows every rebellious Satan.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says it is decreed against him that whoever takes him as a friend will be led astray and led to the chastisement of the burning fire.
verses.5: Al-Mizan addresses doubters of the raising by recalling human creation: from dust, to a small seed, clot, and lump of flesh, complete or incomplete in make; some remain in the womb until their appointed term, then are born, mature, die, or reach senile weakness in which knowledge is lost. Likewise, barren earth stirs, swells, and produces beautiful herbage when watered.
verses.6: Al-Mizan says that Allah is the Truth, gives life to the dead, and has power over all things.
verses.7: Al-Mizan affirms the certain coming of the Hour, when Allah will raise those in the graves.
verses.8: Al-Mizan describes one who disputes about Allah without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating book.
verses.9: Al-Mizan describes one who turns away haughtily to lead others from Allah’s way; he will suffer disgrace in this world and the punishment of burning on the Day of Resurrection.
verses.10: Al-Mizan says this is what their hands have sent ahead, for Allah is not unjust to the servants.
verses.11: Al-Mizan describes one who worships Allah only conditionally: prosperity satisfies him, but trial makes him turn back. He thereby loses both this world and the Hereafter, a manifest loss.
verses.12: Al-Mizan calls invoking besides Allah what can neither harm nor benefit a great straying.
verses.13: Al-Mizan says he invokes one whose harm is nearer than his benefit—an evil guardian and an evil associate.
verses.14: Al-Mizan says Allah will admit those who believe and do good deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow; Allah does what He pleases.
verses.15: Al-Mizan challenges whoever thinks Allah will not assist him in this life and the Hereafter to stretch a rope above himself and sever it, then see whether his effort removes his rage.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as contrasting those who obstinately dispute against truth, those who waver in it, and believers who are guided and blessed.

Regarding (22:3), disputing about Allah without knowledge means ignorantly and persistently speaking about His attributes and acts. Speech is followed by false belief and action, so such a person follows Satan’s path to error. “Every rebellious devil,” rather than the rebellious Devil alone, indicates the many avenues of deception, including devils among humankind, though all evil whispering is rooted in Iblīs. The present tense and “every” indicate continuous, unbounded error: the heart is sealed by it and loses receptivity to truth.

For (22:4), tawallā means taking and following a master and guardian. Al-Mizan understands what is written against the devil as God’s decree that whoever makes him a guardian will certainly be misled from truth and led to the burning fire. The verse can be read as making the devil’s misleading of his follower an established quality. The interpretation that Allah Himself misleads the follower is weak: the Qur’an instead entrusts such followers to Satan, and God has no preceding referent for the relevant pronoun. It is likewise weak to make all the pronouns refer to the ignorant disputant. What is decreed concerning Iblīs also applies to his progeny and assistants; their misguiding and leading to the Fire are his acts.

In (22:5), al-baʿth is the revival of the dead and their return to God. ʿAlaqah is a coagulated clot and muḍghah a chewed lump of flesh. “Complete and incomplete in make” apparently concerns the stage in which the fetus receives shape and form, coinciding with the spirit being breathed into it. The progression from lifeless dust through these stages to a living human makes resurrection possible and removes doubt about it. God chooses which fetuses remain in the womb through the full appointed period; people then emerge as babies and attain full development. Those caused to die and those returned to the worst part of life are distinct groups: the latter reach old age, their faculties weaken, and they lose meaningful knowledge. Barren land is land without vegetation, like extinguished fire; with rain it moves, grows, and brings forth beautiful plants. The earth’s production of plant life thus resembles the womb’s production of animal life.

The creation and ongoing governance of humans and plants in (22:6) show that Allah is al-ḥaqq, Truth in itself, not merely something described as true. He is the reality through which every real being and process exists, and His works show His giving life to the dead and His encompassing power. Verses (22:6)-7 establish resurrection through three connected points: God’s being the Absolute Truth entails that His acts are true rather than vain, so a transient world ending in death requires an enduring Hereafter; His visible giving of life to dead matter refutes resurrection’s alleged impossibility; and His unrestricted power removes any supposed difficulty in its actual occurrence. The Hour therefore certainly comes and Allah raises those in the graves. Calling the Hour “coming” without naming its bringer apparently emphasizes its hidden time and sudden arrival. Although the argument concerns human resurrection, it does not exclude resurrection for other creatures; alternatively, their purpose lies in humankind, whose own end is resurrection. The apparently five conclusions are thus four: the three in (22:6) and the certain Hour and resurrection in (22:7).

Al-Mizan reports from Kashf al-Kashshāf that (22:8) concerns leaders, unlike the followers described earlier, because they lead others astray. Since “knowledge,” “guidance,” and “illuminating book” are separately mentioned, each has a distinct sense. Restricting knowledge to self-evident knowledge is unsound, because disputation is an argumentative process and self-evident propositions need no argument. Perhaps knowledge is gained by rational proof and guidance through sincere worship and divine illumination, or the two may be reversed; the illuminating book is revelation brought by the prophets. Together they indicate the paths of ʿaql, baṣar, and samʿ. God knows best.

In (22:9), turning one’s side is a metaphor for haughty aversion. The person disputes ignorantly and turns away in order to mislead others, characterizing leaders of polytheism. He is threatened with worldly disgrace, as befell leading Meccan polytheists, and burning punishment in the Hereafter. Verse (22:10) makes that disgrace and punishment the requital, or result, of what their hands have sent ahead—ignorant and arrogant disputation meant to mislead. The shift to direct address intensifies the rebuke. Allah wrongs no servant, but gives each what his acts and inner condition call for.

Serving Allah “on the edge” in (22:11) is worship confined to favorable circumstances and directed toward worldly gain. Such a person is stable in religion when good comes, but abandons it completely when afflicted, either taking religion as the source of his misfortune or hoping apostasy will remove it. Like idolaters who worshipped for worldly benefit or protection while denying the Hereafter, he loses this world through his affliction and the Hereafter through turning away from faith. In (22:12), what he invokes besides Allah refers to idols, which cannot harm or benefit because they have neither understanding nor will; the worshipper’s loss proceeds from his own act of worship.

For (22:13), mawlā means a helpful guardian and ʿashīr an associate. On one grammatical interpretation, yadʿū means “he says”: on the Day of Resurrection the idolater will swear that the idol whose harm is nearer than its benefit is an evil guardian and associate. He will say this after seeing that its worship has resulted in everlasting punishment and damnation.

Verse (22:14) contrasts the erroneous and losing disbelieving groups with believers who do good deeds. Allah wills for the latter a noble end: gardens beneath which rivers flow. The contrast prepares for the further account of these groups and God’s judgment between them.

In (22:15), sabab means a means of reaching something and here means a rope; qaṭʿ can mean cutting and also strangling. Al-Mizan regards as most fitting the interpretation that the pronoun in “Allah will not assist him” refers to the Prophet. Meccan polytheists thought his religion would fail, but God supported His Messenger after the migration and spread his religion. The verse rebukes their rage: even if they tie a rope above themselves and strangle themselves, their plotting cannot end God’s help to the Prophet in this world and the Hereafter. Another interpretation makes the pronoun refer to the person who thinks, and takes ascending to heaven and travelling there as an attempt to overturn God’s decree; a third similarly takes assistance to mean provision. Though the third better fits the wording than the second, both are disconnected from the preceding verses. Moreover, man kāna yaẓunnu indicates a continuing thought from the past, supporting the first interpretation.

Finally, kadhālika in (22:16) treats the preceding clear āyāt as representative of the Qur’an as a whole: the Qur’an has been revealed as clear signs like these. The more apparent reading takes “Allah guides whom He desires” as the predicate of an omitted subject: it is true that God guides whom He desires, and no one is guided if He does not will it. Thus even clear verses and arguments do not guide one who hears or reflects on them unless God wills his guidance. The alternative—that the clause is coordinated with “We have revealed it”—is less apparent.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains that the preceding discussion distinguished blind followers and misguiding leaders who dispute about God without knowledge, those who worship on the edge, and believers who do good deeds. The verse declares that God, being witness over all things, will settle the differences among all the religious groups on the Day of Resurrection by decisively separating the followers of truth from those of falsehood.

Those who believe, in contrast with the listed communities, are believers in Muḥammad and the Qur’an. Alladhīna hādū are those who believed in Moses and the prophets before him but not those after him. Their Torah was burnt when Nebuchadnezzar defeated them, leaving them without scripture until Ezra rewrote it after Cyrus defeated Babylonia and freed the Israelites.

The Sabeans cannot be star-worshipers, since star-worshipers would fall among idolaters, whereas the verse distinguishes the Sabeans from those who associate others with Allah. Some exegetes describe them as a community between Jews and Magians, possessing a scripture attributed to Prophet John, the son of Zachariah, and calling each member a Ṣābī. Christians believe in Jesus Christ son of Mary and the earlier prophets; although their canon includes the four Gospels and Church-approved books of the Old Testament, the Qur’an identifies their original scripture as the Gospel (Injīl) revealed to Jesus.

The Magians believe in Zoroaster, though the time of his appearance and the essence of his religion are uncertain because their Avesta was lost after Alexander’s conquest of Persia and rewritten in the Sassanid era. It is nevertheless certain that they posit a good source, Yazdān or light, and an evil source, Ahrīman or darkness, for directing worldly affairs. They regard angels and especially the natural elements, including fire, as sacred and seek nearness to God through angels without making idols of them; they trace these things back to the Creator, Ahūra Mazdā. Those who associate others with Allah are idolaters, including Sabean, Brahman, and Buddhist forms of idolatry, as well as communities with independent idols and rituals.

The repeated inna emphasizes God’s judgment after the long interval between the verse’s subject and predicate. God’s witness over all things means that His judgment is according to truth.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan says that the address apparently concerns everyone capable of seeing, with “seeing” meaning knowledge and realization; it is also possible that the Prophet is addressed specifically, and that it means vision of the heart.

The prostration of the sun, moon, stars, mountains, and other unintelligent beings shows that the intended prostration is existential prostration (al-sajdah al-takwīniyyah): every being, in its whole existence, is subject and humble before God’s sovereignty, might, and grandeur. Thus “whoever is on the earth” includes believers and unbelievers alike, for no one is exempt from this universal, continual, involuntary humility. By naming those in heaven and earth rather than heaven and earth themselves, the verse focuses on creatures, celestial and earthly, intelligent and unintelligent, in this existential prostration.

“And many of the people” must denote a second kind of prostration, since all people were already included among those on earth. This is voluntary and legislative prostration (al-sujūd al-tashrīʿī): casting oneself upon the ground in servitude to God, in conformity with one’s involuntary existential humility. Its opposite is the many who refuse to prostrate. Their punishment is stated instead of their deed to show that chastisement is their own act returned to them: arrogance and refusal of humility necessarily bring an abasement after which there is neither honor nor good.

God has willed this consequence, for all good is in His hand; if He deprives someone of it, no one can provide it. “Surely Allah does what He wills” affirms His absolute power and explains both the inevitability of the chastisement and the finality of that humiliation. Thus, and God knows best, while all beings are existentially subdued before God, people divide between those who voluntarily obey Him in worship and servitude and those who arrogantly turn away; the latter deserve the irreversible abasement. This interpretation also connects the verse to the preceding one.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that the “two adversaries” are the two groups indicated in the preceding verses by God’s decision between the communities and by the contrast between those who prostrate and those for whom punishment is due. Though religions and sects are numerous and internally divergent, they reduce to two sides when measured by truth and falsehood: those who believe in truth and those who deny it. The dual “two adversaries” (khaṣmān) together with the plural verb “who dispute” (ikhtaṣamū) elegantly indicates two opposing camps containing many differing views.

Their dispute concerns their Lord (rabbihim), namely God’s Lordship; all religious differences ultimately return to differing over this attribute. Believers describe God with the names, attributes, and actions worthy of Him, believe in them, and consequently perform righteous deeds. Disbelievers fail to ascribe to Him what befits Him: some posit a partner or child, make nature or the universe the source of creation and existence, reject messengership, or accept some prophets while rejecting others. What unites them is denial of a necessary element of true religion; they are kāfir, those who cover the truth.

After the dispute is settled, the verses begin with the end of the disbelievers: garments of fire are cut out for them and boiling water (al-ḥamīm) is poured over their heads.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that ṣahr means melting, fusing, or dissolving: the boiling water will melt and roast both what is in the disbelievers’ bellies and their skins.
verses.21: Al-Mizan explains that maqāmiʿ, the plural of maqmaʿah, means hammers or pestles of iron.
verses.22: Al-Mizan explains that “from it” means from the fire. “From grief” may further specify that fire, or may state why they seek to leave it. Al-ḥarīq means that which burns, just as alīm means that which hurts.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains that Allah will admit those who believe and do good deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will wear bracelets of gold and pearls and garments of silk.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan explains that a goodly word is speech wholly free from evil (khabāthah), unlike false, invalid, or vain speech. It may be matched with: Their cry in it shall be “Glory to Thee, O Allah!” and their greeting in it shall be “Peace,” and the last of their cry shall be “Praise be to Allah, the Lord of the worlds.” (10:10)

God’s guiding them to goodly words means that He facilitates their way to such speech. Al-Ḥamīd is a name of God; guidance onto the path of the Praised One means that their deeds, like their speech, are praised, commendable, and right. This stands in clear contrast to those who seek to leave the fire in grief but are returned to its burning chastisement.
verses.25: Al-Mizan warns that disbelievers who obstruct Allah’s way and deny residents and visitors their equal access to worship at the Sacred Mosque face a painful chastisement for unjustly inclining to wrongdoing there.
verses.26: Al-Mizan recounts that Allah assigned Abraham the place of the House, commanding exclusive worship of Him and purification of His House for circumambulation, prayer, bowing, and prostration.
verses.27: Al-Mizan says Abraham was to proclaim the Pilgrimage, drawing people on foot and lean camels from every distant way.
verses.28: Al-Mizan states that pilgrims are to witness benefits, invoke Allah’s name over the herd animals He has provided during stated days, eat from them, and feed the distressed needy.
verses.29: Al-Mizan directs pilgrims to remove their ritual dishevelment, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House.
verses.30: Al-Mizan teaches that honoring Allah’s sacred ordinances is better with one’s Lord. Though cattle are lawful except what has been prohibited, idols and false words must be avoided.
verses.31: Al-Mizan commands upright devotion to Allah without association. Associating partners with Him is likened to falling from above, to be snatched by birds or carried by the wind to a far-off place.
verses.32: Al-Mizan states that venerating Allah’s signs proceeds from the piety of hearts.
verses.33: Al-Mizan says they have benefits until a fixed time, then their sacrifice is at the Ancient House.
verses.34: Al-Mizan says that every nation received an act of devotion involving Allah’s name over the herd animals He provided. Since Allah is one, people must submit to Him alone. The humble, who tremble when Allah is mentioned, endure affliction patiently, maintain prayer, and spend from His provision, receive glad tidings.
verses.35: Al-Mizan says that every nation received an act of devotion involving Allah’s name over the herd animals He provided. Since Allah is one, people must submit to Him alone. The humble, who tremble when Allah is mentioned, endure affliction patiently, maintain prayer, and spend from His provision, receive glad tidings.
verses.36: Al-Mizan identifies the sacrificial camels as signs of Allah containing much good. Allah’s name is to be pronounced over them while they stand in rows; once they have fallen, their meat may be eaten and given to the contented poor and the beggar. Their subjection to people calls for gratitude.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as condemning the Meccan polytheists for obstructing believers’ access to the Sacred Mosque, then recalls Abraham’s establishment and proclamation of the pilgrimage and explains its rites.

On (22:25), the commentary identifies those who disbelieved as the Meccan polytheists who rejected the Prophet before the migration, continually prevented people from Islam, and barred believers from circumambulation, prayer, and other worship at the Sacred Mosque. The present tense of yaṣuddūna indicates continuing obstruction despite its coordination with the past tense kafarū. The Mosque has been made equal for all with respect to worship, not ownership: Meccan residents and outside visitors have the same right to worship there. To prevent this violates both people’s rights (ḥaqq al-nās) and, because the way is Allah’s way, God’s rights (ḥaqq Allāh). The threat covers every unjust inclination to violate that right; hence it establishes the unlawfulness of hindering worshippers’ entrance. Al-Mizan considers this contextual reading more fitting than the many grammatical analyses proposed by other exegetes.

On (22:26), Allah’s assigning Abraham the place of the House means revealing to him that it was a point of reference for worship, not a residence. The command not to associate anything with Allah is contextual: it forbids associating others in worship directed to the House, including in sacrificial offerings or the talbiyah. “My House” is exclusively for Allah’s worship, and its purification primarily means cleansing worship there of the spiritual defilement of polytheism and its expressions. Thus Abraham was commanded to worship Allah at that place, worship without association, and establish a pure form of worship for those who come to circumambulate, pray standing, bow, and prostrate. The sequence also suggests the closeness of bowing and prostration. Al-Mizan rejects as unlikely readings that make the assignment an order or instruction merely to settle there, treat an as an infinitival or unstressed particle, divide circumambulators and those standing into visitors and Meccan residents, or make standing, bowing, and prostration all simply refer to prayer.

On (22:27), Abraham—not the Prophet Muḥammad—is addressed, as the context requires. He is commanded to proclaim the ḥajj, the ritual of aiming for the Sacred House. The promised response is that people will come on foot and on lean camels, worn by travel, by many remote roads.

On (22:28), pilgrims come so that they may witness benefits and mention Allah’s name over the livestock He has given them. The benefits are unrestricted and include both worldly and otherworldly goods. Worldly benefits arise as diverse peoples and nations gather despite differences of race, color, custom, and culture, unite upon one truth, one God, and one qiblah, exchange what they need, cooperate to solve their problems, and thereby form an increasingly strong community. Religious agreement is the basis of such cooperation. Otherworldly benefits are the means of nearness to God found in hajj: turning toward Him, leaving ordinary pleasures and occupations, enduring the journey, circumambulating, praying, sacrificing, giving charity, and fasting. Taken together, hajj’s rites resemble Abraham’s passage through monotheism, abandonment of polytheism, and exclusive service to God.

The mention of Allah’s name concerns the sacrifice of livestock—camels, cattle, and sheep or goats—and distinguishes the rite from the polytheists’ practice of invoking idols over their offerings. The Imams interpret the known days as Eid al-Aḍḥā and the three subsequent days of ayyām al-tashrīq. Al-Mizan rejects al-Zamakhsharī’s treatment of invoking Allah’s name as a mere metaphor for sacrifice, since the wording itself concerns remembrance, and also rejects interpreting it as unrestricted remembrance throughout hajj. Eating from the offerings is dispensational, whereas feeding the distressed needy is obligatory.

On (22:29), tafath is the bodily untidiness acquired during iḥrām. Pilgrims are instructed to remove it by such acts as cutting nails and shaving hair, indicating departure from iḥrām, and to fulfil their outstanding vows. According to the Ahl al-Bayt’s interpretation, circumambulating the Ancient House is ṭawāf al-nisāʾ: after leaving iḥrām, the remaining prohibition concerning women is lifted only by this final rite. The House is called ancient because it was the first house established for Allah’s worship.

On (22:30), “that” confirms the preceding legislation of Abrahamic hajj: iḥrām, circumambulation, prayer, sacrifice for Allah, and avoidance of polytheism. Allah’s ḥurumāt are limits that must not be violated; honoring them is better with one’s Lord. Although livestock are lawful, some are forbidden. The continuing form yutlā indicates prohibitions repeatedly recited before this sūrah, rather than a reference to a future recitation such as 5:3. In this context, the chief concern is especially animals sacrificed in another god’s name, though carrion, blood, and pork are also unlawful.

The polytheists retained pilgrimage from Abraham’s religion but sought nearness through idols at the Kaʿbah, Ṣafā, Marwah, and Minā, invoking them when slaughtering. Consequently, avoidance of idol-uncleanness and false words follows from honoring Allah’s ordinances: it prohibits serving idols and the false invocations made to approach them in hajj. The verse says to avoid the uncleanness—that is, the idols themselves—both because they are unclean and to intensify the prohibition so that every relevant form of involvement is included. Al-Mizan regards alternative readings of min as referring to uncleanness produced by idols or to only one aspect of them as contrived and less coherent.

On (22:31), being ḥunafāʾ for Allah means turning away from other gods toward Him, which is identical in sense to not associating anything with Him. It describes the condition required when avoiding idol-directed sacrifices: pilgrimage must turn exclusively toward Allah. The former polytheists’ talbiyah, which admitted a partner allegedly owned by Allah, exemplified what this excludes. The image of one who associates partners falling from above depicts a fall from humanity’s highest rank into the depths of error, where the Devil seizes him as birds seize a falling body; being swept by wind to a far-off place likewise portrays the distance and separation caused by association.

On (22:32), Allah’s shaʿāʾir are signs set up for obedience and worship. Here, in accordance with the Ahl al-Bayt’s interpretation and the following verses, they specifically mean camels driven to Mecca and marked as offerings, rather than every outward ritual or sign of obedience. Reverence for them comes from taqwā of the hearts. Taqwā is the spiritual reality by which one avoids Allah’s wrath through abstaining from what He forbids; it does not lie in external movements, which can be either obedient or sinful, nor in abstract labels such as doing good or obeying God.

On (22:33), the signs are the sacrificial camels, or sacrificial animals generally. Their benefits, such as riding them when needed and drinking their milk, remain until their appointed slaughter at the Ancient House. This accords with the Ahl al-Bayt’s interpretation of an offering brought to the Kaʿbah (5:95). Al-Mizan also records the alternative view that the signs are all hajj rites: on that reading, their benefits are commercial gains until the final destination and rite, circumambulation of the Ancient House.

On the next two verses, mansak most aptly means the devotional act of sacrifice and offering. Sacrificial worship and mentioning Allah’s name over His provision were appointed not only for Muslims but for earlier nations. Since the One who prescribed this rite for all is their one God, they must submit to Him alone and must not seek nearness to other gods by sacrifice. The humble who receive glad tidings are characterized by four qualities: their hearts tremble at Allah’s mention, they patiently bear affliction, they maintain prayer, and they spend from what He has provided. These traits are plainly connected with sincere submission in hajj.

On (22:36), al-budn are fat, heavy camels dedicated as offerings and thus among Allah’s signs. They are to be invoked over while standing in a row, with their feet aligned and forelegs tied. When they fall upon their sides—that is, when they have died—their meat may be eaten; this permission is not an obligation. It must also be given to the qāniʿ, the poor person content with what is given whether or not he asks, and the muʿtarr, the poor person who comes begging. Allah’s subjection of these animals calls for gratitude.

On (22:37), Al-Mizan refutes the notion that Allah benefits from the flesh or blood of offerings. Allah is free of bodily properties, need, and imperfection; what reaches Him is taqwā, in the sense that this spiritual quality rises toward Him, brings its possessor near, and removes the veil between the person and God. Sacrifice therefore has value not because Allah needs it, but because it produces piety and nearness in its offerer.

Takbīr here explicitly means declaring Allah’s greatness. By making animals subject to people, Allah guides them to worship and approach Him through sacrifice, so they should magnify Him for that guidance. Al-Mizan finds this more consonant with the context than the view that takbīr means merely recognizing Allah’s greatness and that guidance means being taught to tame animals generally. Finally, al-muḥsinīn may mean either those who perform good deeds generally or, more particularly, those who give charity in Allah’s way.
verses.38: Al-Mizan states: Allah defends believers and does not love the faithless, ungrateful.
verses.39: Al-Mizan states: Those attacked and oppressed are granted permission to fight, and Allah is able to aid them.
verses.40: Al-Mizan states: Those unjustly expelled for saying, “Our Lord is Allah,” may resist; without Allah’s repelling some people by others, cloisters, churches, synagogues, and mosques where He is remembered would be destroyed. Allah helps those who help His cause, for He is Strong and Mighty.
verses.41: Al-Mizan states: When established in the land, they keep up prayer, pay the poor-rate, enjoin good, and forbid evil; the end of affairs belongs to Allah.
verses.42: Al-Mizan states: If they reject you, Noah’s people, ʿĀd, and Thamūd had already rejected prophets before them.
verses.43: So too did the people of Ibrahim and the people of Lut.
verses.44: Al-Mizan states: The people of Madyan and Musa too were rejected. Allah gave the unbelievers respite, then seized them; severe was His disapproval.
verses.45: Al-Mizan states: How many unjust towns Allah destroyed, leaving them collapsed, with deserted wells and lofty palaces.
verses.46: Al-Mizan states: They should travel so as to gain hearts that understand and ears that hear: true blindness is the blindness of hearts in the breasts, not of eyes.

verses.57:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as the earliest revelation concerning jihad. Muslims in Mecca had long sought leave to resist the polytheists’ torture and persecution, while the Prophet told them he had received no command to fight and urged patience until relief came. Although some identify (2:190) or (9:111) as the first jihad verse, this passage is more fitting: it gives explicit permission, joins it with promises of victory that prepare and strengthen believers, and recalls the fate of earlier unjust peoples. Such elaboration suits the first enactment of a weighty law. Jihad, founded on sacrifice and selflessness, is Islam’s hardest social duty but also its most effective means of sustaining the Muslim community. The announcement begins with Allah’s guardianship of believers, permits their defense against oppression, and warns present oppressors by God’s treatment of earlier unjust societies.

The commentary explains that mudāfaʿah in (22:38) intensifies dafʿ, protection or repulsion, while khawwān and kafūr denote extreme treachery and ingratitude. Though initially addressed to Muslims at the time of revelation, “those who believe” extends to all Muslims and thus to all subject to jihad. The faithless and ungrateful are the polytheists: Allah entrusted them with true religion through their fiṭrah and through His messenger so that they might attain felicity in both worlds, yet they betrayed that trust through denial and disbelief. Surrounded by visible and hidden blessings, they failed to thank Him through worship. Allah’s defense of believers against them anticipates the permission to fight. It implies His love of believers for their faithfulness and gratitude, and by defending them He defends the religion they bear; He is their Guardian and Protector against His enemies.

In (22:39), “permission is given” introduces a new injunction: permission to fight. Those upon whom war is made are the same believers mentioned previously, now described in terms that show what they may do. The common passive reading, yuqātalūna, means those fought by the polytheists and shows that the polytheists initiated war. The bāʾ in bi-annahum gives the reason: permission is granted because they are oppressed, as the next verse explains. The unnamed giver of permission magnifies Him. Likewise, stating merely that Allah is able to help them does not expressly affirm help, but shows that helping them is no burden to the One powerful over all things; it indirectly promises His aid.

Verse (22:40) identifies their oppression as expulsion from their Meccan homes without right. The polytheists did not necessarily carry Muslims out bodily; by harassment, torture, and disturbance, they compelled them to leave their homes and possessions, some for Ethiopia and others for Medina. The clause “except that they say: Our Lord is Allah” is an unconnected exception: they were expelled solely for professing what was true, exposing the polytheists’ distorted judgment. The alternative that treats the profession as the sole “just cause” does not fit, because the verse means that no justification existed. Although the expelled are specifically the Muhājirīn, they stand for the believers generally, who form a united body.

The verse thereby justifies jihad as protection of religious communities against enemies seeking to extinguish divine guidance. Without Allah’s repelling some people through others, houses of worship—ascetics’ cloisters, churches, Jewish places of worship, and mosques—would be demolished, and religious rites and worship abolished. Their mention represents religion because such places are its signs, reminders, and enduring public image. This repulsion is broader than warfare: it includes the natural human practice of defending life and well-being. God has equipped creatures with means of defense and humans additionally with reason, by which they preserve what benefits them and acquire what they need to flourish. Fighting is the final remedy, used only after other means fail; it removes one thing to preserve another, as hardship is endured for eventual benefit. It is thus one branch of a natural custom, attributed to Allah because He repels people by people to preserve His religion. The verse also indicates that some form of defensive law existed in earlier religions.

Allah’s promise to help whoever helps His cause is emphatic: He aids those who protect His religion through jihad. The commentary holds that He fulfilled this by helping Muslims against enemies so long as they aided His cause and elevated His name. His strength means none can weaken or obstruct what He wills, and His might means none can encroach upon or rival His sovereignty.

Verse (22:41) again describes the believers collectively, not particular individuals. To establish them in the land is to give them freedom to choose their way of life without obstruction or rival. If so established, they will found a righteous society that maintains prayer, gives zakāh, enjoins good, and forbids evil. Prayer and the poor-rate are singled out for their centrality among devotional and financial duties. This is a universal description of believers, extending to all Muslims until the Day of Resurrection, not only to the Muhājirīn; jihad is not restricted to a group, and the believers’ intrinsic nature is righteous even when veiled.

The early Medinan society initiated and supported by the Anṣār, then spread across Arabia, exemplified the verse through its establishment of prayer, zakāh, good, and resistance to evil. The Muhājirīn did not establish such a society independently of the Anṣār. Restricting the verse to the Muhājirīn would require making it about either the four Rightly Guided Caliphs in a Sunni reading or Imam ʿAlī in a Shiʿa reading, which would undermine the passage’s sense. Moreover, certain historical acts of the first generation, especially of the Muhājirīn, cannot be called reviving truth or abolishing falsehood, even if attributed to individual ijtihād. The verse concerns the community as a whole. “Allah’s is the end of affairs” reinforces His promise to aid believers against the enemies of religion who oppressed them.

The next three verses console the Prophet: rejection of a prophet is not new, since the peoples of Noah, Hūd’s ʿĀd, Ṣāliḥ’s Thamūd, Abraham, Lot, and Shuʿayb’s Madyan also rejected their prophets. They also threaten current deniers with the exterminating divine punishment that followed earlier rejection. The wording says Moses himself was rejected rather than “the people of Moses,” because the Israelites believed in him, whereas Pharaoh and his people denied him. Allah gave those unbelievers imlāʾ, respite, then overtook them in punishment; His nakīr is His severe repudiation of their disbelief.

Verse (22:45) expands this severity through ruined unjust towns whose roofs collapsed before their walls, abandoned wells whose users had vanished, and lofty or plastered palaces left without inhabitants. Wells and palaces evoke, respectively, nomadic and settled peoples. Travel in the land is urged in (22:46) so that people may reflect on these remains, recognize that past nations perished through polytheism, turning from God’s signs, arrogance toward truth, and rejection of messengers, and thereby avoid disbelief. Those capable of independent reflection gain hearts that understand; those unable to do so may heed the compassionate adviser and preacher who distinguish benefit from harm, above all God’s Book and Messenger.

The contrast between heart and ear therefore concerns two paths to truth: independent intellection and following one whom it is permissible to follow. In reality both are acts of the heart, understood as the rational soul bearing cognitive faculties. Its understanding is its vision; one who neither reflects nor listens is blind-hearted. Physical blindness may be partly compensated by a cane or guide, but blindness of heart has no substitute. “Breasts” as containers of hearts is an allegory, just as attributing understanding to qalb is allegorical when it properly belongs to the soul.

Those who mockingly demand that punishment be hastened are answered in (22:47) that Allah never fails His promise. This may concern the Meccan polytheists and their defeat at Badr, or a promised final judgment between the Prophet and his people that has not yet occurred. A day and a thousand years are alike to Allah: He neither discounts the short nor is overwhelmed by the long. He does not hurry from fear of losing the opportunity, but forbears until the wicked complete their degrees of wretchedness, then seizes them at an appointed time that neither advances nor delays. Thus the interpretations that make the day a thousand-year day of the Hereafter, or merely a day whose torment feels like a thousand years, do not accord with the verse’s beginning and sequel. The statement also reassures the Prophet and rebuts his opponents’ mockery.

Verse (22:48) evidences that divine forbearance: many unjust towns received respite before Allah overtook them. Their return to Him means He need not hasten punishment, for nothing can escape its final return. It is not a repetition of (22:45): that verse describes God’s forbearance as an attribute, while the first-person declaration here conveys that God Himself opposes those who oppose His Prophet.

In the following verses, the Prophet is commanded to announce that he is a clear warner, then to state the consequences of faith and denial. Forgiveness is the reward of faith; honorable sustenance, Paradise with its blessings and pleasures, is the reward of righteous deeds. Those who strive against the signs exert their utmost effort to invalidate them and extinguish their light, as though trying to outstrip God; their enduring recompense is the flaming Fire.

On (22:52), tamannā ordinarily means to suppose or desire something one likes, possible or impossible, and umniyyah is the pleasing imagined form of that desire. It can also mean recitation. If it means a messenger’s or prophet’s inward plan and aspiration to advance religion and persuade people, Satan interferes by tempting people, inciting wrongdoers and corrupt persons, and impeding the prophetic effort. Allah then removes Satan’s interference, makes the effort succeed, and manifests truth. If it means recitation, Satan casts doubts and disputes among listeners to corrupt believers’ faith, but Allah annuls them through prophetic refutation or further revelation.

The commentary rejects the common account that rasūl is one given revelation and charged to proclaim it, while nabī receives revelation without such a duty. Since the verse contrasts the two, this would make the nabī here not a rasūl; but “We did not send” itself means commissioning one to convey a message. Traditions from Ahl al-Bayt instead distinguish them by the mode of revelation: a messenger sees and speaks with the angel in waking revelation, while a prophet receives revelation in dreams. The distinction that messengers bring a new shariah while prophets follow an earlier one is also rejected: only Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad brought divinely prescribed codes, though the Qur’an calls many others messengers, and no proof supports the proposal. The alternatives that messengers alone possessed an official scripture, or some written text, face the same problem.

The shift from “We” to the explicit name Allah in “Allah annuls” and “Allah establishes” emphasizes that the irresistible God performs these acts. Repeating Satan’s name likewise emphasizes that the caster is the insignificant Devil, whose schemes are void before God.

In (22:53), disease of the heart is defective understanding that fails to accept truth it should admit: doubt and suspicion. Hardness of heart is the loss of gentle qualities—humility, compassion, modesty, and love—that assist comprehension. A diseased heart quickly apprehends truth but slowly accepts it; a hardened heart is slow in both, while both readily receive satanic whispers. Satanic interjections obstruct truth and prophetic work, but can also be ascribed to Allah insofar as nothing operates in His kingdom without His permission and whatever is attributed to Him has a good, beneficial purpose. They are trials within His universal practice by which the felicitous attain salvation and the wretched damnation; for diseased and hardened hearts specifically, the trial completes their wretchedness, in accordance with God’s universal fostering of all.

The lām in “so that He may make” gives the purpose: Satan’s casting occurs under God’s authority so that servants may be tested and the doubtful and denying may be tempted and misled. Fitnah is a trial resulting in deception and error; those with diseased hearts are doubting disbelievers, and the hard-hearted are the defiant deniers among them. The unjust are in shiqāq baʿīd, an opposition that sets them far from truth and its people; they are the deniers, or perhaps deniers together with doubters.

Verse (22:54) gives the corresponding purpose of Allah’s nullifying Satan’s castings and establishing His signs: those given knowledge may know that what the messenger or prophet envisioned and sought is truth from the Lord, believe in it, and become humble and softened in heart. The pronoun “it” refers to the messenger’s or prophet’s aim, not necessarily to the Qur’an. Alternatively, the opening conjunction may join the clause to an omitted purpose, as Qur’anic usage sometimes joins an expressed consideration to one left implicit. Allah acts thus because He guides believers to the straight path through this instruction.

Verse (22:55) does not concern every disbeliever alive at revelation, since some later believed, but the leading Quraysh figures who died unbelieving, like those described as unresponsive to warning. They will doubt the Qur’an until the Hour suddenly seizes them, or until its chastisement comes. A barren day, ʿaqīm, is one followed by no other day; though it could mean the Day of Resurrection or the day of an individual’s death or a community’s destruction, the following verses establish the former. The Day and its chastisement are alternated because either compels confession of truth. Its suddenness means no plot or preparation can evade it; its barrenness means no later opportunity remains to correct the past.

Finally, the closing verses say that Allah’s kingdom will become manifest on the Day of Resurrection, though it has always been His. This is not metaphorical. Created beings possess only formal, conventional authority granted by Him, whereas Allah alone possesses real authority through existential ownership. On that day the veil of apparent authority is removed, leaving only His real and exclusive dominion. Judgment belongs to Him alone because judgment is a branch of dominion, and no other being will retain a share of authority. His judgment places believers who do good in gardens of bliss, while those who disbelieve in and arrogantly reject His signs and revelation receive a disgraceful chastisement.

verses.62: Al-Mizan states that Allah is the Truth, while what is called upon besides Him is falsehood; He is the High, the Great.
verses.63: Al-Mizan states that Allah sends down water from above, making the earth green; He is Subtle and Aware.

verses.66:
Al-Mizan introduces verses (22:58)–66 as continuing the preceding message: they promise reward to those who migrated and were killed fighting in God’s way or died, encourage fighting, and promise divine aid to the oppressed retaliator. It notes the distinctive sequence in which verses 58–65 each end with two of God’s Names after Allah. If Huwa is counted as a Name, though it may merely be a repeated pronoun, the verses contain sixteen Names: Huwa, Khayr al-Rāziqīn, al-ʿAlīm, al-Ḥalīm, al-ʿAfuww, al-Ghafūr, al-Samīʿ, al-Baṣīr, al-ʿAliyy, al-Kabīr, al-Laṭīf, al-Khabīr, al-Ghaniyy, al-Ḥamīd, al-Raʾūf, and al-Raḥīm. Verse 66, together with the statements that Allah is the Truth and owns all in heaven and earth, effectively adds al-Muḥyī, al-Mumīt, al-Ḥaqq, and al-Mālik or al-Malik, making twenty Names.

On (22:58), the commentary says the promise concerns the Muhājirīn expelled from their homes by force and oppression. Migration alone does not qualify one for reward: it and being slain or dying must be “in Allah’s way,” with sincere intention for God rather than wealth, power, or other worldly aims. The goodly sustenance is the bounties of the Hereafter—Paradise—received after death or being slain; Allah’s being the best Giver of sustenance grounds the promise.

For (22:59), mudkhal is most likely a noun of place derived from idkhāl, not a maṣdar. The unconditional description of the entrance as pleasing them indicates the utmost satisfaction of all they desire. This entrance expounds the goodly sustenance: God will give them a welcome entrance despite their earlier unwilling, forced expulsion by the polytheists. He knows what will please them and prepares it, while His forbearance explains why He does not hasten to punish their oppressive enemies.

On (22:60), dhālika means that the matter is as stated, and ʿiqāb is retaliatory pain following an earlier act. Retaliation “with the like” means equal treatment, and the phrase that the person “has been oppressed” qualifies the initial affliction as unjust. In the context of permission for jihad, Allah’s aid apparently means support and victory in battle for the oppressed. It may also mean legislating the right to exact equal redress for unjust loss or damage, as in the authority granted to an unjustly slain person’s heir in (17:33). On this second reading, pardon and forgiveness explain God’s permission: He removes the evil consequence inherent in such unpleasant infliction, provided it is equal retaliation by the oppressed against the oppressor. It is therefore not a sin. Thumma does not here mark temporal succession, but adds the qualification of oppression.

The commentary rejects an interpretation attributed to some exegetes under which one first retaliates against a criminal and is then oppressed again, whereupon God aids him and pardons his first retaliation, although patience and forgiveness would have been better. That reading makes thumma temporally separate retaliation from the later baghy, leaving the retaliation unqualified even though the interpretation assumes it followed criminal oppression. It also makes the promised aid an existential act of vengeance that is not invariably seen in reality, and makes fighting the polytheists an application of a verse whose reading nevertheless prefers pardon, creating a contradiction.

A translator’s note qualifies the discussion: Qur’anic uses of ʿāqaba occur in contexts of unjust affliction, so the term itself can include retaliation through battle, whereas baghy is not always negative, though it is here. The note also holds that naṣr apparently denotes existential support through dominance, so the objection that such aid is not always manifest would extend to other promises of divine aid. It suggests that the verse may concern those who retaliated before permission for jihad, and, in light of (42:39-43), offers the possibility that one attempts to retaliate for an initial injustice but is then oppressively suppressed.

For (22:61), the entrance of day and night into one another is their replacement and progressive expansion over the other. It pictures God’s customary making of one opposite overcome another and thus the oppressed overcoming the oppressor. God hears what people say and sees what they do; He sees the oppressed person’s right taken and hears his complaint and supplication through his lisān al-ḥāl—his inner tongue, language of condition, or existential capacity.

For (22:62), dhālika refers to God’s aid, or possibly to both that aid and the preceding explanation of it. The exclusive contrast may mean that Allah is wholly true and idols wholly false, or that Allah alone possesses truth in Himself and all other truth exists only by His grant and validation; what the deviators rely on, including idols, has no truth of its own. Either way, Allah alone has authority in takwīn and tashrīʿ, while what others serve cannot act. His Highness means that He dominates without being dominated, and His Greatness that nothing can abase or humiliate Him; both follow from His unabolishable, unending Truth.

For (22:63), “sky” means what is above. Water descending from above and greening the earth demonstrate God’s all-encompassing power, and the latter event is explained by His being Subtle and Aware. Verse (22:64) apparently further complements this proof: because He owns all in heaven and earth, He directs His kingdom as He wills in accordance with His subtlety and awareness. It may instead be an independent justification for (22:62). Allah’s self-sufficiency means that He needs none of His acts, while His praise-worthiness means that they are all beautiful, commendable, and beneficial; their benefits belong to creatures, not to Him.

Verse (22:65) is further proof of universal power. The contrast between what is on earth and ships at sea indicates land as distinct from water; together with heaven, it shows that God has subjected heaven, earth, land, and water to people. “Heaven” means what is above, including meteors and thunderbolts, which He prevents from falling except by His permission. Compassion and mercy complete the account of His bounty toward people.

Finally, the past tense of bringing people to life in (22:66) concerns worldly life, while the later revival is the eternal life after the Resurrection, not temporary life in barzakh. Life, death, and resurrection are among God’s greatest bounties and complete His grace; humanity’s response is therefore described as ungrateful.

verses.78:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as commanding the Prophet to proclaim his call, establishing its truth against polytheism, then summing up religion for believers in worship and good deeds before closing with the command to strive in God’s way.

For (22:67), mansak means nusuk, an act of worship, rather than a place of worship, since it is described as something performed. “Every nation” means successive nations through history, not the various peoples living alongside the Prophet, because his message is universal. The verse apparently addresses People of the Book or polytheists who challenged Islamic rites absent from earlier laws. Each nation had rites suited to it, but God replaced them for later nations with rites better fitted to their more advanced capacity; the earlier rites were thus abrogated. Their prohibition from disputing the Prophet rests on this rational point despite their refusal to accept his authority. It also consoles him: he should ignore their criticism and continue calling to his Lord. “Straight” qualifies guidance metaphorically, as guidance leads to the right path.

The contention in (22:68) is, in this context, continued dispute about the differing rites after their justification, not every religious contention or a dispute specifically about sacrifice. The Prophet is told not to return their argument, but to say that Allah best knows what they do, thereby preparing for divine judgment. God will judge their differences about truth and its people on the Day of Resurrection. His knowledge of their acts is established because their acts belong to what is in heaven and earth, all of which He knows. Their deeds are inscribed in a book, so they are neither lost, forgotten, nor mistaken when He judges; recording them is easy for Allah.

The polytheists worship what has neither a proof sent by God nor any known reality. The distinction between a divinely sent authority and knowledge allows that some truths are known directly without argument. Al-Mizan rejects the restriction of the former to transmitted religious proofs and the latter to rational proofs: a sent authority is general enough to include revelation to prophets and rational arguments cast upon hearts. The unjust have no helper: this warns that none can save them from punishment, while, in the argument’s immediate context, naṣīr also means the proof or knowledge that would assist them. Thus their injustice itself entails that no proof or knowledge supports their worship.

When clear signs are recited, denial and reluctance are evident on disbelievers’ faces, and rage nearly drives them to attack the reciters. They regard the Qur’an as bad and avoid hearing it, but the Fire is worse than what they reject: Allah has promised it to the disbelievers, and it is an evil destination.

The parable of (22:73) exposes the alleged gods’ impotence in creation and governance. Even gathered together, they cannot create a fly; if a fly takes something from them, they cannot retrieve it or repair the harm. Thus they cannot rightly be invoked or worshiped. In context, the seeker is the idol attempting to create the fly or recover what it took, and the sought is the fly; the idols are weaker than an animal regarded as among the weakest yet possessing some power and intelligence.

To estimate Allah as He deserves is to give Him the status required by His exalted attributes: to take Him alone as Lord and worship none besides Him. The polytheists instead made powerless idols their lords, worshiping them in fear and hope despite their inability even to create or withstand a fly. They thereby degraded God by equating Him with such idols, and indeed preferred the idols over Him. Allah is absolutely Strong, without weakness, and Mighty, without defeat or humiliation; these names directly contrast with the idols’ weakness and abasement and establish Him as the source of creation and governance.

Allah’s choosing of messengers is deliberate selection of those fittest and choicest for the task, not a random appointment. Human beings inherently need guidance to the felicity and perfection for which they were created; this need is effectively a request that Allah, the Hearing and Seeing, perceives and answers. Since not everyone is fit to connect with the transcendent realm, He chooses angelic messengers to receive revelation from Him and convey it to human messengers, and human messengers to convey it to people. The following verse further explains the necessity of this selection and entails the messengers’ infallibility.

“What is before them and what is behind them” refers, on its apparent meaning, to the angelic and human messengers. God watches the whole course of revelation: what is behind each messenger lies between that messenger and God, while what is before angelic messengers is their delivery to human messengers and what is before human messengers is their delivery to people. He protects revelation throughout this stream from forgetfulness, distortion, alteration, and satanic interference. Hence the messengers are infallible in receiving, preserving, and transmitting revelation. All affairs return to Allah not merely at a future time, but essentially: they belong to and depend absolutely on Him, so nothing is concealed from His knowledge.

Bowing and prostrating command the prayer; serving the Lord includes other prescribed worship such as pilgrimage and fasting. “Do good” comprises the remaining laws of the sharīʿah, through which society’s good, individual felicity, and true life are realized. The verse therefore enjoins the entirety of Islamic legislation, its ritual and other rules alike.

Jihād is the exertion of one’s utmost capacity to repel an enemy. Though commonly used for fighting, its enemy may include Satan, the evil-commanding soul, and whatever threatens a person; the Prophet referred to resisting one’s nafs as al-jihād al-akbar. Here its apparent sense is the broadest one, because striving in the way of Allah includes all that pertains to Him. It must be undertaken purely and sincerely for God, without associating another with Him.

God’s choosing the believers, removing hardship from religion, and giving them Abraham’s faith are divine favors without which they could not attain this religion. The removal of hardship includes both laws difficult in themselves and laws that become difficult in particular circumstances; the sharīʿah is therefore easy and gentle. Abraham is their father as Muslims because he was the first described as submitting to God, counted his followers as belonging to him, and prayed that he and his sons be kept from idols—his “sons” thus being Muslims rather than polytheists. God Himself named them Muslims before the Qur’an and in it, a favor showing His acceptance of their islām, whether understood as their submission or their adherence to Islam.

The Messenger’s witnessing over them and their witnessing over people concerns people’s deeds and explains the preceding favors. Since God has bestowed these blessings, they must establish prayer, give the poor-rate—representing devotional and financial rites—and hold fast to Allah in every affair, obeying His commands and avoiding His prohibitions without severing themselves from Him. He is their mawlā, either their master or helper; a servant cannot abandon his master, nor a weak person his helper. His being their Guardian therefore grounds these commands, while His excellence as Guardian and Helper consoles and fortifies them.

The majority interpretation applies being chosen, being Muslims, and being witnesses to all believers and the whole Muslim community, because the preceding address is to believers. Al-Mizan, however, maintains that ijtibāʾ in its real sense makes a servant mukhlaṣ, wholly and exclusively for God, and that this, along with the real meanings of islām and holding fast to God, belongs only to a few. The verse nevertheless describes the whole community by these terms because it contains people truly marked by them, just as the Qur’an sometimes describes all Israelites by qualities possessed by some among them.
